transcript.text: I manage a small retention team at a subscription company. We can phone only 50 customers a month, out of about 1,200. I want to know which 50 to call. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. A call costs us about the same for every customer; a customer who stays is worth their monthly spend. We do not know yet whether a call changes anyone's mind. [shares customers.csv]

I'll look at the table first so the options I give you are grounded in your actual numbers.

Here's what your table says and how I'd read the problem. The real decision isn't "who is most likely to churn" — it's "which 50 slots return the most money." Since a call costs the same whoever picks up, the ranking should be predicted churn risk multiplied by that customer's monthly spend. Your base churns at 17.4% a month, and the customers who left carry 7,282.75 of monthly spend between them. Fifty calls cover a small slice of 1,200 people, so the choice of names is most of the value. The signals are already visible: basic plan churns at 22.4% against 11.1% for plus, and customers with 3 or more support tickets in the last 90 days sit at 24.5% versus 15.5% for those with none. Tickets and plan pull in different directions on spend though, and no single rule weighs them against each other — that's what a model buys you. I also checked the columns for leakage: nothing looks written after the outcome, and signups run from 2022-01-01 to 2025-10-31, so I can validate on the latest customers rather than grade on the ones the model already saw. One honest gap: you said you don't know whether a call changes anyone's mind, and this table can't tell us — there's no record of who was called. A risk score finds who is likely to leave, which is not the same as who is persuadable. The cheapest fix is to leave a few of each month's 50 uncontacted at random, so the calling itself proves its worth. The three options below are a model-built list, a rules-only list today, and the brief that sizes and tests the programme. Which fits how your team works?

choices.title: Score all 1,200, hand the team a ranked list of 50
choices.what: Train a churn model on signup_date, segment, city, plan, tenure_months, monthly_spend and support_tickets_90d against churned_next_month, validate it on the latest signups, then score all 1,200 and rank by risk x monthly_spend. You get: A ranked 50-name call list with each customer's churn risk and value at stake, plus a check on how many churners the list captures versus picking 50 at random. Trade-off: It ranks who is likely to leave, not who a call can save - so I would build in a small randomly held-aside group so you learn lift while you call. Effort: One build now; a refreshed list each month, retrain every 1-3 months.

choices.title: Value-at-risk shortlist from the rules you can see now
choices.what: Rank the base right now on the risk signals already visible (plan, tickets, tenure, spend) and score each customer as risk x monthly_spend. You get: A defensible 50-name list today and the revenue it puts under the phone. Trade-off: Blunter: it cannot weigh the signals against each other, so some slots go to customers who would have stayed anyway. Effort: Fastest: minutes, nothing to retrain.

choices.title: Work out what 50 calls a month is actually worth, and prove it
choices.what: Size the prize from your table (churn runs at 17.4%, and customers who left carry 7,282.75 of monthly spend), then set the 50 calls up as a small randomised test: risk-ranked customers split into called and deliberately-not-called, with the measure, the sample size needed and the stop rule. You get: A yes or no on whether the phone programme earns its keep, so you know whether to keep the calls at 50 a month or push for more capacity, and what the team does with each list either way. Trade-off: You spend part of this month's capacity learning rather than saving, and the answer takes a couple of months of calls. Effort: A brief now; it then runs alongside your normal calling.

transcript.text: I am the operations manager of a home appliance retailer. Our support complaints went up by about 30 percent since March, by my own count from the weekly reports. My director wants an AI model to fix this. We have no dataset: the tickets sit in our helpdesk system as free text with a date and an agent name, and nobody has labelled the reasons. I decide what the support team works on next month. What should we do?

Here's how I read it: your director asked for a model, but the real question is narrower and older — *what changed in March*. A 30% rise in a helpdesk is almost never a mystery that needs prediction; it's two or three causes (a faulty batch, one product line, a delivery or install problem, a warranty policy change, a new promotion) that grew faster than the rest. Prediction models answer "will this happen"; you need "what is already happening, and what should the team stop doing to it next month."

Two things I'd flag before anything else. First, I'm reading your 30% as a raw count of tickets per week, not complaints per unit sold or per order shipped. If sales or the installed base grew since March, part of that rise is just more appliances in homes — that changes the whole story, so if you have monthly sales or shipment counts, they're worth having next to the tickets. Second, agent names in the data can mislead: a few agents can look like the cause simply because they picked up the surge. The honest answer on the AI model: it can't be built yet, and not because of the volume of tickets. With no reason labels there is nothing to learn from and nothing to check a model against. Labelling the reasons is the step that unlocks both your plan for next month and any model later, so I'd do that first and let the model be a second phase. Pick whichever of these fits what you want to hand your director. Each one needs the same thing from you: an export from the helpdesk covering roughly December through now — ticket text, date, and product or category, order number, repeat-contact flag if the system can attach them.

choices.title: A decision brief for you and your director
choices.what: You share the ticket export (text, date, plus product/category or order number if the helpdesk can attach them). I tag complaint reasons from the text, compare March-to-now with the months before, and write it up as a decision brief: ranked causes, what each would take to fix, and a straight answer on whether an AI model is the right next move. You get: A short brief you can hand your director: the causes behind the rise, what the support team should work on next month in priority order, and what an AI model would actually need before it could help. Trade-off: It reasons from the export and your own weekly reports rather than a statistical model, so numbers are as good as the data you can pull. Effort: Medium: needs the ticket export, then a written brief.

choices.title: Find the actual cause of the 30%
choices.what: You export the tickets (text, date, and product/category or order number if the helpdesk can attach them). I clean that export, tag every ticket with a reason category read from the text, then compare March-to-now against the months before to rank which reasons, products and weeks drove the increase. You get: A ranked list of the two or three causes worth the team's time next month, with ticket counts and share of the rise for each. Trade-off: Needs a real export from the helpdesk and one pass of reason-tagging, so it is a few days of setup before the first number, not an instant answer. Effort: Medium: one export, one tagging pass, then numbers.

choices.title: Build the labelled ticket table you do not have
choices.what: Turn the raw export into a tidy, de-duplicated ticket table: one row per ticket, parsed date, reason category, product/category, agent, repeat-contact flag. This is the dataset your director is implicitly asking for. You get: A reusable table that answers any future question (by product, by agent, by week) and the foundation any model would need. Trade-off: Gives you structure rather than an answer today; you still need the cause analysis to decide the fix. Effort: Small to medium: export shape and rules agreed once.

transcript.text:
I'll start the brief and get one piece of domain depth on it first.

Brief started. Here is its substance — this is what you'd put in front of your director. **The line for your director.** The cause of the March rise is findable in days from tickets you already have, and a model is the right *second* step, not the first: with no reason labels there is nothing for a model to learn from and nothing to check it against. **First, is service actually worse?** Your 30% is a raw count of tickets per week. Three possible outcomes: the rate is flat, and the rise is growth rather than a problem — that changes your answer completely; the rate is up everywhere, a genuine deterioration; or the rate is up only in certain categories or products, which is the best case because it's targeted. I'm assuming you can get weekly order or shipment counts out of another system; if you can't, say so, because that's the first gap to close. **The four usual suspects, in the order they show up in free text.** One product or batch failing (same category, near-identical phrasing, dates clustered after March) — most common and most expensive to troubleshoot. Delivery or install damage: "arrived dented", "missing parts", "installer broke the door" — not a product problem, owned by a different team. A policy change: warranty terms, a charge, a returns rule announced around March, which reads as repeat contacts and escalations. Mix and season: a spring push on cooling or laundry, or a promotion driving volume, not defects. You'll know which story is true within a week. **Next month's team plan, before you even know the cause.** Protect capacity on two fronts: reopened and repeat tickets, which cost you two or three touches for one customer; and any suspected batch or product fault, which should go straight to a hold/replace route instead of re-troubleshooting, because diagnosis burns hours that can't fix a bad batch. One thing would sharpen the brief a lot: when you export tickets, can the helpdesk also give you product or category, order number, and whether a ticket is a repeat contact — or is it text, date and agent name only?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

I'll close the open points with my own judgment and lock the brief.

Brief locked and complete. Here it is, written so you can hand it over with your name on it. **Part 1 — Read the number before you repeat it.** Three things could make "up 30%" misleading, and each costs under a day to check. First, the denominator: this is a raw count of tickets per week, and complaints per hundred units shipped is a different number. If sales grew since March, part of the rise is simply more appliances in more homes. Second, how the report is counted: does one customer reply creating a second ticket stay one ticket, or does a reopen count again? A change in that default, or a new intake channel switched on around March, can lift a weekly count with no change in service at all. Third, the shape: is it a step in one week or a gradual climb? A step points at an event — a product launch, a policy change, a batch, a channel change. A climb points at mix, growth or season. Note which it is before you say anything to your director. Write the codebook first, about ten reason tags — product fault, damaged on arrival, install problem, missing or wrong part, delivery timing, warranty or policy dispute, repair turnaround, billing or return, other, and unable to tell. "Unable to tell" is real information; keep it. Have two people code the same fifty tickets independently and compare. If agreement is poor, the tags are the problem, not the people — and this matters beyond this exercise, because a codebook is the ceiling on any model you build later. Then compare the mix since March against the baseline mix. One bucket carrying the growth gives you a cause and an owner. Growth spread evenly everywhere is a system problem: process, capacity or the report's definition. Use the agent name last and cautiously — whoever absorbs a surge looks like its cause. **Part 3 — Next month's workload, which you can set today.** Put a fix-it-first queue on repeat and reopened contacts: a second touch costs two to three times and means the first answer didn't resolve. Route anything matching a suspected batch or fault pattern to a hold-or-replace decision rather than troubleshooting, because diagnosis cannot repair a bad batch. Assign a named owner outside support for anything pointing at delivery, installs or policy — support owns the ticket, not the cause.

(That is the short version. Ask me about any part and I will go deeper.)

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

The brief is settled, so here is the sheet you can run this week without waiting on anybody. **Day 1, ask for two exports.** From the helpdesk: one row per ticket, December to today, with the date created, the full text including the subject line, the agent, and whatever else the system offers (channel, product field, order number, a reopen or repeat flag) — take what exists, don't wait for what doesn't. From wherever your orders live: weekly order or shipment counts for the same weeks, plus a dated list of anything that changed around March — promotions, new product launches, warranty or returns policy, a new chat or phone channel. **Days 2–3, code by hand.** Write the ten tags down first: product fault, damaged on arrival, install problem, missing or wrong part, delivery timing, warranty or policy dispute, repair turnaround, billing or return, other, unable to tell. Take roughly sixty tickets from January–February and sixty from March onward, picking every fifth one in date order rather than the interesting-looking ones — cherry-picking will point at whatever you already suspect. Have a second person code the same fifty independently and compare notes before you go further. **Day 4, read what you get.** One tag carrying most of the increase is your cause, and it usually names its owner outside support. Growth spread evenly across all tags is not a product story: it's capacity, process, or the weekly report's definition changing. Either way you now have a countable basis for next month's queue priorities, not an impression. **The line for your director:** the tagging is the model's training data, done by hand first so it can be checked — the automated version becomes phase 2, scoped against labels that already exist. Roughly three or four hours of work, and no procurement. When you have the export, drop it here and I'll run the before-and-after mix comparison and give you the chart with the numbers.

findings.text: The reported rise is a raw weekly ticket count, so it can be inflated by more orders, more customers, or more channels rather than worse service. Normalizing complaints against sales, orders, installs, or traffic is essential before judging it as a service-quality problem.
An AI model is premature because the tickets have no labelled reasons; building now would chase noise and could hide the controllable causes.

Can the helpdesk and operations data be aligned to orders shipped, products sold, installations, website traffic, promotions, warranty changes, and channel releases so complaint rates can be compared week by week?

In home appliance retail, step-change complaint rises usually come from batch faults, delivery or install damage, new products, promotions, seasonal categories, website or channel changes, and warranty or policy changes. The brief should test these against changes in mix, volume, timing, and agent patterns.

What are the cheapest triage levers now: can the team quickly spot highest-volume or highest-severity complaint buckets, repeated issues, and whether particular products, orders, deliveries, installs, channels, or policy changes dominate them?

Before modelling, the minimum labels are a small stable set of reason and context tags: why the complaint happened, what it concerns, whether it relates to sale, delivery, install, warranty, promotion, seasonal category, channel, or repeat contact, plus severity and outcome.
